papers.title: Rapid trait adaptation has contrasting effects on different dimensions of stability under environmental change
papers.abstract: Environmental change alters species growth rates and, through species interactions, can produce complex effects on community functioning and composition. Because functional traits mediate both environmental responses and competition, rapid trait adaptation may modify these effects, but its consequences in multispecies communities remain unclear. We used a trait-based model of competitive communities to test how adaptation affects the mean and diversity of species growth responses to environmental change, and how this influences functional and compositional resistance (how unaffected the community is by the environmental change) and resilience (how well it recovers after it has acclimated to the altered environment). Adaptation altered response variance more strongly than the mean by changing the balance between environmental optimisation and competition-driven trait divergence. As a result, adaptation strongly increased compositional stability, but had less clear effects on abundance. Adaptation also generated a trade-off between resistance and resilience: faster adaptation improved resistance but reduced resilience as communities were displaced less by the environmental change and thus recovered less. Overall, adaptation can be stabilising, but higher adaptation rates do not necessarily produce greater stability across all stability components.

papers.title: WildObserve: Camera-trap image review software that learns species labels during annotation
papers.abstract: Motion-activated camera traps are an effective tool for monitoring animals, but a single study can produce millions of images, which must be analyzed before they yield data. The burden of analyzing them has led many teams to automate the work with computer vision. These models lose accuracy on images unlike those they were trained on, however, and a general model may not use the categories a project needs. Adapting a model to a project usually requires at least one of the following: many labeled images per species, programming expertise, a graphics processing unit (GPU), or uploading images to a remote server. I describe WildObserve, a desktop application that adapts to each project without any of these requirements. Before a reviewer sees an image, MegaDetector finds animals, people, and vehicles and marks images that are likely empty, and SpeciesNet suggests a species for each animal. WildObserve keeps SpeciesNet's feature vector for each animal, so as the reviewer confirms or corrects labels, a project model (a logistic regression on those features) retrains in about a second on an ordinary laptop, learning the project's own species list and names. Images stay on the user's computer, model outputs and human decisions are kept separate, and exports record review and model provenance. On the Caltech Camera Traps dataset, WildObserve processed 8.1 images/s on an Apple M1 Pro laptop with Core ML (1.5 images/s on its CPU), species suggestions included. At a 0.5 threshold, it found animals in 97.1% of animal images but also put a box on 48.0% of images labeled empty. On 1,467 animal crops from 14 categories, SpeciesNet alone reached 0.919 balanced accuracy. The project model reached 0.886 with three labels per category and 0.937 with 25, and 0.931 on camera locations absent from its training labels; built on features from DINOv2, a general-purpose image model, it reached only 0.784 with 50. On the Oregon Critters dataset, released after SpeciesNet was trained, SpeciesNet reached 0.751 and the project model passed it with only ten labels per category (0.783). WildObserve gives a project species suggestions in its own categories, from a model it trains simply by reviewing, without writing code, needing a GPU, or sending images elsewhere.

papers.title: Contrasting relationships between evolved consumer diversity and productivity for essential vs. substitutable resources
papers.abstract: Any mechanistic biodiversity-ecosystem functioning theory must explain how biodiversity in natural communities arises, which requires an evolutionary metacommunity perspective. Using a model of adaptive evolution of competitive metacommunities in landscapes with spatially heterogeneous supply of two resources, we studied the evolution of resource-uptake specialization as a function of resource type (substitutable/essential) and trade-off shape between resource-uptake affinities (generalist-/specialist-favouring). We identified "critical essentiality" as a key phenomenon separating parameter regions with fundamentally different biodiversity--ecosystem function relationships. Specifically, while greater spatial heterogeneity in resource supply increases biodiversity, this comes at the cost of reduced productivity when resources are essential. Moreover, when resources are essential, both generalist- and specialist-favoring trade-offs select for phenotypes that prevent efficient resource partitioning, leading to low resource use efficiency and consumer biomass - despite often high species richness. In contrast, when resources are substitutable, a specialist-favoring affinity trade-off selects for phenotypes that partition resources efficiently, promoting a metacommunity of only two species characterized by high functional diversity, resource use efficiency, and biomass. Overall, our analyses thus suggest that conditions promoting the evolution of diverse consumer communities often do not engender higher functional richness, consumer biomass, or resource use efficiency.

papers.title: Demographic stochasticity can drive population variability even in large populations
papers.abstract: Demographic stochasticity is generally expected to contribute little to population variability when census abundance is large, because random demographic events are increasingly averaged across many individuals. This expectation, however, depends on how evenly individuals contribute to reproduction. In many natural populations, reproductive success is highly skewed, so that a large census population can coexist with a much smaller effective number of breeders (Nb). Although Nb is commonly used as a genetic measure of contemporary effective size, it also summarizes variation in reproductive contribution and may therefore contain information about demographic variability. Here, we develop a female-based age-structured theoretical framework linking Nb to temporal variability in mature population abundance, with N denoting the census number of mature females and Nb the effective number of female breeders. Recruitment variability arises from non-Poisson reproductive variation and environmental stochasticity, and its transmission to mature abundance is described by a life-history coefficient, {gamma}, determined by survival, maturation, and the contribution of overlapping cohorts. When the Poisson component of recruitment variance is negligible and Nb/N is sufficiently small, the coefficient of variation in mature abundance, CV[N], can be approximated from Nb, environmental variability, and {gamma}, with little additional information from census abundance. This approximation does not require specification of the functional form of the relationship between adult abundance and recruitment. Stochastic age-structured simulations closely reproduced the analytical prediction, even when additional demographic stochasticity in survival was included. Substantial fluctuations in mature abundance occurred at census sizes on the order of 105 when Nb was small, whereas overlapping cohorts buffered recruitment fluctuations. Because Nb can be estimated genetically from samples of a single cohort, the framework provides a direct link between genetic monitoring and population dynamics. More broadly, these results show that large census abundance alone does not guarantee weak demographic variability and highlight the potential of genetic data to inform expected population fluctuations when detailed demographic information is limited.

papers.title: Stemflow as a Storm-Driven Pathway for Fungal eDNA Transport
papers.abstract: Stemflow transports water and biological material from forest canopies to the stem base, yet fungal studies of this flux have largely relied on microscopy of conidia. We used ITS2 metabarcoding to characterize fungal environmental DNA (eDNA) in stemflow from 15 trees - five each of American beech (Fagus grandifolia), sugar maple (Acer saccharum), and tulip poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera) in a closed-canopy forest in northeastern Ohio, USA. Stemflow was sampled during eight rain events in the leafless season (November 2024-May 2025), along with simulated bark and gutter washes to assess near-collar and collector signals. Natural stemflow communities were compositionally distinct from both controls and occupied greater ordination space. Ascomycota dominated across all samples, with Parafenestella, Cytospora, Microcera, Nectria, and Aureobasidium among the most abundant resolved genera and 13 of the 25 most abundant taxa differed significantly among host species. Woody-plant-associated endophytes, canker fungi, and saprobes dominated ecological guild composition. Storm event explained 28.6% of taxonomic variation, host tree species 24.1%, and their interaction 10.0%. Guild composition was more strongly structured by host species (35.4%) than storm event (20.4%). Lichenized fungi and lichen-associated fungi were detected. Thus, leafless-season stemflow integrates broad bark-associated fungal eDNA, including recurrent lichen-derived material, beyond the morphologically distinctive conidia captured by traditional methods. Stemflow eDNA therefore offers a minimally invasive means of monitoring canopy fungal diversity and the strong host and temporal filtering of DNA exported from woody surfaces.

papers.title: Ecological coupling of foraging and thermoregulation in harvester ants from a tropical deciduous forest in southern Mexico
papers.abstract: Diurnal ectotherms in hot and dry ecosystems face an acquisition trade-off between maximizing collective energy intake and minimizing individual exposure time. We employed optimal foraging and thermoregulation models to examine the surface foraging and thermoregulatory strategies of Pogonomyrmex barbatus foragers in response to habitat warming in a tropical deciduous forest. Foraging activity was evaluated using field-based thermal performance curves (fTPCs) for individual foraging speed and collective foraging success. Thermoregulation was assessed through indices of thermal unsuitability, as well as thermoregulatory effectiveness and exploitation. Our results show that afternoon conditions were significantly hotter and drier than those in the morning. Furthermore, the decoupling of fTPCs was dynamic; while the optimal temperature (Topt) for individual foraging speed remained stable at 44 degrees C, the Topt for collective foraging success shifted from 35 degrees C in the morning to 41 degrees C in the afternoon. This shift in foraging strategy, driven by stressful afternoon conditions, was reflected in a transition of the thermoregulatory strategy. Specifically, the probability of foraging activity decreased as thermal unsuitability increased, with a lower baseline in the afternoon. The thermoregulatory exploitation dropped from 94% in the morning to 63% in the afternoon. Based on thermoregulatory effectiveness, foragers transitioned from an active thermoregulatory strategy in the morning to a thermoconformist strategy in the afternoon while foraging on the surface. So, the observed colonies optimized the balance between individual foraging speed and collective foraging success through a thermoregulatory strategy that was primarily spatial in the morning and strictly temporal in the afternoon. A comparison with historical data from the same site reveals a 40% contraction in the total daily foraging window since 2013.

papers.title: Beyond diversity: A whole system view of vegetation's control of erosion
papers.abstract: Streambank erosion degrades both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, and riparian buffers are among the most widely used tools to control it. Yet most of what is known about how riparian vegetation controls erosion comes from one or two-species systems, which overlook the diversity of riparian communities and species interactions (competition and facilitation) that may shape the root systems that bind soil. We used a streambank mesocosm experiment to test whether plant species richness alters root traits, and whether root traits and species interactions reduce erosion. We established 85 mesocosms ranging from unvegetated controls to six-species polycultures, measured root biomass, length, volume, and diameter, quantified species interactions with relative yield totals (RYT), and measured erosion rate with a jet erosion test. Vegetated mesocosms eroded significantly less than unvegetated controls (t = 4.05, p = 0.023). Richness did not affect most root traits, although mean root diameter decreased as richness increased ({beta} = -0.0225, p = 0.047). RYT ranged from competition (RYT 1), yet neither interactions nor any root trait was directly associated with erosion rate. However, RYT was negatively associated with soil moisture ({beta} = -0.196, p = 0.010). Piecewise structural equation models showed that erosion was best explained by a pathway linking species presence, root length, and soil moisture (AIC = 39.27; Fisher's C = 11.27, df = 12, p = 0.506). Panicum virgatum increased root length, whereas Lolium multiflorum and Echinochloa crus-galli reduced it; longer roots were associated with drier soil (standardized {beta} = -0.31, p = 0.005), and wetter soils eroded more slowly (standardized {beta} = -0.39, p < 0.001). Which species were present mattered more than how many, and plants were linked to erosion through soil moisture rather than root traits alone. Species selection for riparian buffers may need to consider effects on soil moisture as well as rooting extent, particularly as droughts followed by intense storms become more common under a changing climate.

papers.title: Temperature and management reduce the abundance of the invasive Argentine ant (Linepithema humile)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Argentine ant (Linepithema humile) is among the world's worst invasive species. In the Donana Biological Reserve (Spain), it is associated with human structures that provide the mild, moist conditions it needs within the hot, dry scrubland. We evaluated a habitat-modification treatment, predicting that removing this suitable habitat would eradicate the invader locally. Over an 18-year period, we monitored ant communities at a treated and an untreated site, at different distances from the human structures, before and after treatment, and analysed how temperature and worker numbers affected encounters at baits between the Argentine ant and native ants. RESULTS: Distance to the human structures shaped ant communities at both sites, but only the treated site changed after treatment. There, the Argentine ant decreased close to the human structure and almost disappeared farther from it, whereas the endemic Cataglyphis tartessica and C. floricola recovered, especially close to the structure. At baits, the outcome of encounters depended mainly on how temperature changes favoured each species relative to its maximum activity temperature: Cataglyphis spp. displaced the Argentine ant in the morning, as temperature increased, and the Argentine ant recovered the baits in the late afternoon. Numerical advantage favoured only the Argentine ant. CONCLUSION: Habitat modification reduced the Argentine ant and allowed endemic ants to recover, but did not eradicate the invader, which persisted at low abundance 13 years after treatment. In protected areas, habitat management should be combined with eradication, monitoring and prevention of spread.

papers.title: Life-history and connectivity shape the viromes of a migratory and river-resident galaxiid
papers.abstract: Migration can increase population connectivity and gene flow but may also facilitate pathogen transmission among hosts and habitats. The way life-history strategies shape viral diversity in closely related freshwater fishes remains poorly understood. Here, we used metatranscriptomics to compare the viromes of two fish in the family Galaxiidae with contrasting life-history strategies: amphidromous [i]nanga (Galaxias maculatus) and river-resident Gollum galaxias (Galaxias gollumoides). We analysed 54 pooled libraries derived from 416 individuals collected across 27 sites spanning multiple catchments and fish-passage barriers in southern New Zealand. A total of 13 novel fish-associated viruses were identified from five viral families (Astroviridae, Circoviridae, Coronaviridae, Hepeviridae, and Picornaviridae). Virome composition differed markedly between species, with only a single virus-positive pool detected among [i]nanga, whereas Gollum galaxias harboured 11 novel viruses, with circoviruses dominating the virome. No fish-associated viruses were detected in post-larval juveniles of either species, and alpha diversity did not differ significantly among catchments, sites or positions relative to fish-passage barriers. However, beta diversity analyses revealed significant spatial structuring of viral communities among sites and catchments, indicating localised variation in virome composition. Contrary to our predictions, the migratory species exhibited substantially lower viral diversity than the river-resident species. The absence of detectable viruses in juveniles, combined with the greater viral richness of the longer-lived Gollum galaxias, suggests that host longevity and cumulative environmental exposure may be important drivers of virome assembly. These findings demonstrate that host life-history strategy influences virome composition and reveal unexpectedly low viral diversity in a globally widespread migratory galaxiid, providing new insights into virus-host ecology and connectivity in freshwater fishes.

papers.title: Assessing fish biodiversity and community structure in the Ganjiang River using eDNA metabarcoding
papers.abstract: Hydropower development has emerged as a major driver of global environmental change, causing significant ecological damage to freshwater ecosystems and threatening aquatic biodiversity. However, the impact of cascade dams on fish communities in large river systems remains poorly understood, particularly in biodiversity hotspots such as China. Here, we used environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding to assess the spatiotemporal patterns of fish diversity and community structure in the Ganjiang River, the largest tributary of the Yangtze River, in relation to cascade hydropower development. We collected water samples from 19 sites along the main stem and major tributaries in both wet and dry seasons, and analyzed the eDNA data using high-throughput sequencing and advanced bioinformatics pipelines. Our results revealed significant seasonal and spatial variations in fish diversity and community composition, with lower species richness and distinct assemblages in the impounded sections upstream of the dams compared to the downstream reaches. The fish communities were strongly influenced by environmental factors such as water temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, and nutrients, which exhibited complex interactions with dam operation and land use practices. Spatial scale analyses further indicated that the impact of dams on fish diversity was most pronounced at the local scale, but also detectable at the regional scale. Our findings provide novel insights into the ecological consequences of cascade hydro-power development on fish communities and highlight the importance of considering spatial scales and environmental heterogeneity in assessing the impacts of human activities on freshwater biodiversity. Our study demonstrates the power of eDNA metabarcoding as a cost-effective and non-invasive tool for biodiversity assessment and conservation planning in large river systems facing multiple stressors and knowledge gaps.

papers.title: Recording context and data splitting can inflate acoustic re-identification accuracy across species and studies
papers.abstract: 1. Re-identifying individual animals (re-ID) from their calls with machine learning (ML) could extend individual-based monitoring to species and areas hard to survey by capture and marking, and published studies often report re-ID accuracy above 90%. Two methodological practices can inflate these values: (1) attributing calls to individuals by territory, nest, tag or station, tying each animal to its own recording conditions, and (2) randomly splitting individual clips into training and test sets, allowing recording context to be shared between them. Each effect has so far been documented only in single-species studies. 2. We implement four diagnostics of how methodological choices affect re-ID accuracy: (1) splitting clips by recording session; (2) background tests using ambient recordings without the animal; (3) within-recording permutation and paired-clip tests where animals share recordings; and (4) open-set tests with thresholds set on other individuals. We applied them to 13 public datasets from nine species (eight birds, one bat), using BirdNET, 19 other neural networks trained on animal or general sound and 16 trained on human speech, each with one classifier. 3. Under session splits, BirdNET re-ID accuracy ranged from 0.16 to 0.97. Within one year, ambient sound alone carried substantial identity information for territorial chiffchaffs (BirdNET balanced accuracy 0.71, against 0.79 for song); background identification exceeded chance for 35 of 38 embeddings and controls. Count-matched random clip splits raised mean accuracy by 0.20 to 0.51 in 18 comparisons across three species. Where several animals shared recordings, only one of three datasets showed clearly that re-ID rested on the animal rather than the recording. With unfamiliar animals present and thresholds calibrated to target 10% stranger acceptance, across 36 neural networks and two scoring methods on wild session-split datasets, the highest median share of known birds' calls accepted and correctly named was 46%, using nearest-clip scoring with four enrolled birds; test-stranger acceptance could exceed the target. No neural network beat BirdNET on every dataset, and network rankings depended on layer choice. 4. The diagnostics need no new models and apply wherever a dataset holds what they require: session labels, background recordings, shared recordings or enough individuals. Re-ID accuracy reported without them can substantially overstate what acoustic re-ID achieves, and should not be used to plan population monitoring until they are applied.

papers.title: Specialization between foliar fungal endophyte and plant communities decreases toward the tropics
papers.abstract: Associations among species are hypothesized to become fewer and more specialized toward the tropics. However, evidence for the latitudinal specialization gradient (LSG) remains mixed and restricted to plant-animal and host-parasite models, with increasing recognition that our understanding of LSG is often complicated by differences in species richness and sampling effects. Here, we tested whether specialization between foliar fungal endophytes - fungi that live within plant leaves - and their plant hosts increased toward the tropics by surveying 1,539 plants that spanned a 55-degree latitudinal gradient in Central and North America. Contrary to expectations, endophytes and plants formed a greater number of associations that were more evenly distributed toward tropical latitudes and were thus less specialized, even after accounting for differences in endophyte and plant community structure. Endophyte-plant communities were most specialized where evaporative demand and plant richness were low, and where water availability and primary productivity were high. Our findings show a reversed LSG where the specialization between endophytes and plants decreased toward the tropics and provides evidence that many species of endophytes can coexist even when there is high overlap in their host niches.

papers.title: Reduced skeletal density and mechanical resistance in mangrove-associated Pocillopora sp. corals
papers.abstract: Coral skeletal integrity underpins reef habitat complexity and coastal protection, yet it remains unclear whether corals persisting in chemically variable marginal habitats, such as mangrove-associated reefs, maintain sufficient mechanical resistance to withstand physical disturbance. We combined micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) morphometric analysis with compression testing to quantify skeletal microarchitecture and compressive mechanical performance of Pocillopora sp. skeletons collected across a habitat gradient at Low Isles, Great Barrier Reef, from mangrove-associated sites to exposed reef sites. Baseline skeletal properties varied among sites, with the Proximal Reef site having the densest and least porous skeletons, while mangrove-associated sites had the most porous skeletons. Similarly, Proximal Reef skeletons exhibited two-to-three-fold greater compressive stiffness and peak force than mangrove-associated skeletons. Percentage object volume was a stronger predictor of compressive stiffness than surface area-to-volume (S/V) ratio, indicating that bulk skeletal density better captured load-bearing capacity than surface architectural complexity. Structural failure mode also differed markedly among habitats: mangrove-associated skeletons underwent catastrophic fragmentation of their open, porous framework, whereas Distal and Proximal Reef skeletons failed through discrete crack-plane propagation while largely maintaining overall structural coherence. These results indicate that the physiological stress tolerance associated with mangrove habitats occurs alongside reduced mechanical resistance and more destructive failure modes, suggesting a potential trade-off between chemical stress tolerance and structural investment. Assessments of resilience in marginal coral populations should therefore consider skeletal mechanical performance alongside physiological tolerance, particularly as climate change intensifies storms and alters hydrodynamic disturbance regimes.

papers.title: Can carcasses cause environmental nucleic acid pollution? Implications for interpreting environmental RNA/DNA survey results
papers.abstract: Environmental nucleic acid (eRNA and eDNA) metabarcoding is a promising tool for biodiversity assessment as it supports low-cost, noninvasive biological surveys. A critical challenge for eRNA/eDNA analyses is accounting for nucleic acid contamination that can compromise the accuracy of biomonitoring results. The primary aim of the current study was to examine carcasses as potential sources of eRNA/eDNA contamination, a contribution that remains poorly understood. Using Japanese medaka (Oryzias latipes), we quantified the detectability and persistence of carcass-derived eRNA/eDNA in water through two complementary experiments: (i) a shedding study comparing eRNA/eDNA release from live and dead individuals and (ii) a decay experiment measuring temperature-dependent degradation from 4 to 34 {degrees}C. Dead fish released detectable amounts of both eDNA and eRNA, indicating that eRNA-based surveys cannot fully eliminate carcass-derived signals. Arrhenius-based analysis showed that eRNA degradation was more temperature-dependent than eDNA degradation. These results suggest that eRNA may improve temporal resolution for recent organismal presence under warm conditions, whereas carcass-derived eRNA may persist under cold conditions and complicate interpretation of positive detections. Overall, eRNA may help reduce carcass-related false positives, particularly in warm conditions, but should be paired with temperature-aware sampling strategies and temporal replication during colder periods.

papers.title: Delayed bleaching-induced coral mortality limits reef recovery after a marine heatwave
papers.abstract: The increased frequency and intensity of coral bleaching events expose reefs to disturbance-recovery cycles that threaten their long-term dynamics. Understanding the impact of thermal stress requires evaluating coral mortality and recovery rates after disturbances. By integrating two long-term monitoring datasets, we examined coral mortality and recovery patterns at 13 sites in Mo'orea, French Polynesia, following the 2019 bleaching event, the most severe heat stress on record for the island. The maximum accumulated heat stress (AHSmax) varied from 5.76 to 6.26 {degrees} C weeks and enabled a direct analysis of heat-stress-related mortality. One year after bleaching, Pocillopora mortality increased with AHSmax, reducing mean coral cover from 35% to 17%. Regardless of AHSmax, Acropora mortality was high at all sites (median: 84%), reducing mean cover from 5% to 1% and indicating greater heat tolerance of Pocillopora than Acropora. Within four years after the bleaching event, no recovery occurred, and coral cover further declined relative to pre-bleaching levels. This decline was stronger for sites exposed to more intense heat stress. The impact of colony size was assessed by tracking 3090 individual Pocillopora colonies over six years and estimating size-dependent mortality and growth with a Bayesian mixed model. Immediately after the bleaching event, large Pocillopora corals exhibited a higher probability of complete and partial mortality than smaller colonies, highlighting size-specific consequences of bleaching. Even three years after the heat stress ended, large Pocillopora corals remained stressed, as evidenced by the continuously high probability of partial mortality. The lack of recovery observed here may be related to increased spatial competition with macroalgae. The disappearance of large fecund colonies and high mortality of coral recruits could have catastrophic consequences for the resilience of Mo'orea's reefs.

papers.title: JEPA-SORT: World-Model Embeddings Improve Deep-Sea Multi-Object Tracking on Visually Homogeneous Fauna
papers.abstract: Protecting deep-sea sessile communities as Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) requires accurate estimates of their spatial distribution and abundance. Existing computer-vision detection methods require careful calibration to avoid counting errors; multi-object tracking (MOT) theoretically offers a more robust alternative. In practice, however, poor lighting and turbidity limit the efficacy of purely kinematic MOT algorithms in deep-sea environments. At the same time, the intra-species visual homogeneity typical of deep-sea scenes means traditional per-frame appearance features are often too weak to maintain stable identities in deep-association MOT algorithms. In this paper we introduce JEPA-SORT, an MOT algorithm that injects V-JEPA 2.1 embeddings into detection-to-track association, to show that video world-model embeddings - which capture not only physical appearance but spatiotemporal trajectory across viewpoints - can help maintain stable identities on visually homogeneous specimens. We provide a benchmark of twelve ROV transects surveying deep-sea sessile communities and evaluate JEPA-SORT against standard MOT algorithms across a range of simulated optical environments. We also propose the Biodensity Utility Metric (BDU), which measures tracker performance in the context of downstream ecological modeling. JEPA-SORT outperforms all benchmarked trackers on IDF1, MOTA, and BDU and is competitive on specimen-count accuracy. Ablations indicate its advantage stems primarily from the discriminative power of world-model embeddings on visually homogeneous footage.

papers.title: Land use and climate warming interact to reshape global avian biodiversity through ecological filtering and homogenisation
papers.abstract: Land-use and climate change are dominant drivers of terrestrial biodiversity change, yet are usually analysed separately although they co-occur and may interact. We integrated global bird assemblage records from PREDICTS with temperature anomalies and species' ecological characteristics to test how land use modifies biodiversity responses to climate warming across three dimensions: local abundance and richness, compositional dissimilarity among assemblages, and species occurrence across ecological groups. Land use modified warming associations for both abundance and richness. Relative to primary vegetation, warming associations were more positive in low-intensity agriculture for both responses, but more negative for richness in high-intensity agriculture and urban land. Predicted richness remained below the reference, defined as primary vegetation at temperature anomaly 0, across all modified land uses, with the largest declines in high-intensity agriculture (-17.9%) and urban land (-21.8%). Within land-use classes, greater warming exposure was generally associated with higher compositional similarity, consistent with warming associated biotic homogenisation. Occurrence models revealed ecological filtering: broad-niched generalists were favoured in warmer modified habitats, whereas range-restricted habitat specialists were filtered out under intensive land use and warming. Conservation assessments should therefore integrate land-use-warming interactions with changes in assemblage composition and ecological strategies, particularly in agricultural and urban landscapes where warming further disadvantaged range-restricted specialists.

papers.title: More fruits, more frugivores, but not necessarily more visits: findings from two tropical plant-avian frugivore communities
papers.abstract: Fruit resource availability can influence the local abundance of avian frugivores through bottom-up regulation, but whether greater resource availability translates into higher visitation rates to fruiting trees remains poorly understood. Greater fruit availability could increase visitation by supporting larger frugivore populations, or reduce visitation to individual trees if increases in frugivore abundance are not proportionate to those in fruit availability or if frugivores distribute their foraging effort. Understanding these relationships can provide insights into the relative role of abundance and trait-based mechanisms in structuring plant-frugivore communities. We compared fruit availability, avian frugivore abundance, and frugivore visitation rates on fruiting trees across two protected wet tropical forest sites: Anamalai Tiger Reserve in the Western Ghats and Namdapha Tiger Reserve in the Eastern Himalaya. Specifically, we quantified the availability of bird-consumed fruits across one-ha patches, estimated local abundances of major frugivore groups, and tested whether visitation rates on individual fruiting trees were related to frugivore abundance, body mass, and degree of frugivory. We found that small-seeded fruit availability was significantly higher in Anamalai than in Namdapha. Local abundances of several relatively small-bodied frugivore groups, including bulbuls, barbets, fairy-bluebirds, and mynas, were also higher in Anamalai. However, visitation rates of several frugivore groups on individual fruiting trees were higher in Namdapha. Visitation rates across all avian frugivore species were associated with frugivore abundances only in Anamalai, and not associated with body mass or degree of frugivory in either site. Thus, although greater fruit availability was likely associated with higher frugivore abundance, this increase in abundance did not consistently translate into higher visitation rates at individual fruiting trees, which provides some support for the resource dilution hypothesis. Our results highlight the importance of considering fruit resource availability and frugivore abundance when examining variation in tropical plant-frugivore interactions.

papers.title: Data-driven identification of the ecologically relevant climatic windows and climate summaries with StatClim model
papers.abstract: Climate affects biological processes and organisms. It is extensively recorded, and its effects are frequently studied. Climatic variables are recorded as time series of measurements, but these are often summarized as long-term averages, throwing away biologically relevant information. Subsequent analyses can therefore miss important climate effects or suffer from low predictive power. Here, we propose a new method, StatClim, inferring the most informative climatic summary from the data. Instead of taking a fixed arbitrary summary of a time series, StatClim automatically estimates the beginning and width of a climatic window and simultaneously calculates data aggregation, which best predicts a response variable. We implemented the proposed approach as a Bayesian hierarchical model in Stan. We illustrated the potential of StatClim on published data on mast seeding of Fagus sylvatica. StatClim correctly identified known climatic windows relevant for this tree species, but also uncovered that mast seeding is triggered by high temperatures within these windows. We demonstrated flexibility of the model to account for complex data structures, we ran power analysis showing the ability of the model to identify climatic effects even with modest datasets, and we evaluated its false positive rate, which is lower than 0.01. We discuss the advantages and limitations of StatClim. Compared to existing alternatives, it is suitable for hypothesis testing and offers important advances, such as estimation of the type of aggregation. In combination with existing methods, StatClim will facilitate data-driven use of climatic and microclimatic data and therefore discovering so far unknown climatic effects on biological processes and ecosystem functioning.

papers.title: Modeling the Impact of Contamination on Microbial-Enzyme Dynamics and Soil Function
papers.abstract: Globally, contaminated soils pose serious risks to agriculture, biodiversity of ecosystems, and human health. Although a variety of monitoring and remediation methods have been developed over the years, there remains a lack of theoretical modelling to better understand the impact of contamination on soil carbon in a microbially-mediated system. In this study, we develop a model which incorporates contaminated soil organic carbon, uncontaminated soil organic carbon, dissolved organic carbon, microbes, extracellular enzymes, and CO2, to explore how different amounts of contamination and modes of contamination (pulse and press) affect microbially-mediated carbon flux within both vegetated and barren environments. The model represents contamination as a pool of contaminated soil organic carbon that is more resistant to microbial degradation than uncontaminated soil organic carbon. The results show that, in barren environments, the amount and type of contamination has no notable impact on the soil system. In contrast to this, in vegetated environments, plants mitigate the impact of large contamination inputs with differences in outcome depending on the amount and type of contamination.

papers.title: Self-generated oxygen limitation drives coral outcomes during marine heatwaves
papers.abstract: Marine heatwaves cause massive, but often patchy coral bleaching. Why neighboring colonies often respond differently remains unresolved. Here, we show that interactions between metabolic demand and flow-mediated resupply generate heterogeneous oxygen microenvironments inside branching corals under heat stress. During the 2023 and 2024 Red Sea heatwaves, high-frequency in situ measurements revealed hypoxic to near-anoxic interbranch conditions despite well-oxygenated surrounding seawater. In 2023, neighboring colonies developed divergent oxygen regimes preceding paling and bleaching; in 2024, stronger and earlier thermal stress was associated with recurrent nighttime near-anoxia before tissue disintegration and mortality. A physics-based three-dimensional fluid-metabolism model reproduced these patterns. Oxygen depletion and coral impacts emerged when metabolic oxygen demand exceeded flow-mediated resupply. Organism-scale variability in oxygen regimes may explain divergent coral fate under shared heatwave exposure.

papers.title: Low Symbiodiniaceae diversity across Acropora hosts on the Central Pacific atoll Kiritimati
papers.abstract: The transformative impacts of global bleaching events are now a ubiquitous feature of coral reefs, often resulting in taxonomically simplified coral assemblages that can persist long-term due to ongoing ocean warming, heatwaves, and localized anthropogenic stressors. Understanding to what extent these processes shape symbiont biodiversity continues to be a major knowledge gap. Here, we examined Acropora host and symbiont communities on Kiritimati (Republic of Kiribati), seven and a half years after the 20152016 El Nino-associated marine heatwave, which caused a near total loss of the genus in the atoll's shallow reefs. We quantified Acropora cover and growth-form composition at 37 sites spanning a gradient of local human disturbance and characterised Symbiodiniaceae communities using ITS2 DNA metabarcoding from 109 coral tissue samples at 13 of the sites. Corymbose and tabular Acropora growth forms remained evenly represented across the atoll and cover declined with increasing human disturbance. Symbiodiniaceae communities were dominated by Cladocopium with 93 % of colonies associated with a single ITS2 profile. Communities were homogenous, with low diversity and insignificant differences amongst growth forms, but slight differences across disturbance levels. DNA barcoding of the PaxC intron identified the majority of host colonies as most similar to Acropora granulosa (62 %) and Acropora hyacinthus (24 %). Although dominance by a single symbiont lineage is common among Acropora species across the Pacific, the low Symbiodiniaceae diversity observed at Kiritimati contrasts with the substantial within- and among-lineage diversity documented elsewhere. The depauperate Symbiodiniaceae communities observed in this study may thus represent a lasting legacy of the 2015-2016 disturbance, with the recovering Acropora assemblage representing an early stage of community reassembly drawing from a potentially depleted environmental symbiont pool.

papers.title: Unstable Heteroresistance as a Stepping Stone to Stable Resistance via Compensatory Mutations
papers.abstract: Antibiotic heteroresistance, a trait in which a drug-susceptible population harbors a rare resistant subpopulation, has been presented as an unstable intermediate state on the way to classic stable antibiotic resistance. However, the timescales and pathways under which this could occur has not been examined. Extending a recombination-based model of copy- heteroresistance to include compensatory mutations, with rates and costs from experimental estimates, we simulated populations across thousands of generations of growth with {beta}-lactam exposure. In the first days a founder population survives by one of two paths, either amplifying the resistance gene to a high copy-number or gaining compensatory mutations and staying at low copy-number. However, both paths converge over weeks to months on the same low-copy compensated state, which would be indistinguishable from classical resistance. Importantly, the ending state would provide no information as to the route taken: an isolate sequenced afterward carries no sign of the intermediate amplified state. With the parameters estimated and across a wide range of parameters, we find that amplification-mediated heteroresistance can be a transient stepping stone across lethal selection that leaves no sequence trace in surviving isolates.

papers.title: First nationwide mosquito surveillance in Northern Irish wetlands reveals presence of Culex pipiens/molestus hybrids
papers.abstract: While mosquito invasions and associated pathogens are increasingly prominent in Europe, evidence gaps remain for many northerly regions where proactive management interventions may be most effective. At the regional periphery of Europe, there remains a significant knowledge gap concerning mosquito vector distributions in Northern Ireland. This study aimed to address this major gap by systematically surveying larval and adult mosquito populations in key habitats (ponds, reedbeds, saltmarsh, wet grasslands, wet woodlands, and urban gardens). We further identified environmental drivers of important vector species abundance and screened collected specimens with molecular techniques to identify presence of cryptic human-biting vector species. In Northern Ireland, mosquitoes (including potential bridge vectors of West Nile and Usutu viruses) were found to be widely distributed. Between May and August 2025, a total of 2430 mosquitoes (951 adults and 1479 larvae) were collected over 196 trap nights and 76 larval collections. Collections encompassed 17 species, with Culex pipiens/torrentium being the most widely distributed and abundant taxon recorded. Mosquito abundances were greatest in reedbed habitats, related negatively with rainfall and peaked in June and July. A subset of Culex pipiens/torrentium mosquitoes were identified to species/biotype level using PCR, with the majority (89.3%) identified as Culex pipiens pipiens and 9.3% as Culex torrentium. Importantly, the first detections of Culex pipiens/molestus hybrids (1.8%) on the island of Ireland were found. This work underscores the wide, yet previously undocumented abundance and distribution of potential zoonotic vectors in Northern Ireland and provides an important baseline for management planning and future research, while contributing to broader understandings of environmental population drivers and distributions.

papers.title: A sample-to-identification workflow to monitor animal and plant biodiversity using metabarcoding and real time analysis
papers.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a transformative tool for biodiversity monitoring, offering a non-invasive means to detect and identify species across various ecosystems. However, despite its potential, current eDNA methodologies have significant limitations, including limited sensitivity, restriction to a specific taxonomic group, lengthy processing times, the need for specialized laboratory conditions and equipment, as well as computational bottlenecks in equipment, connectivity, and algorithms. Overcoming these limitations is crucial for the real-time monitoring of a high number of taxa in field-based scenarios. Here we present an integrated eDNA workflow from extraction to data analysis that mitigates several of these challenges through several technical innovations. Our approach adapts the Tagsteady protocol to Nanopore sequencing, integrates multiplex PCR for simultaneous plant and animal detection, and introduces RTBioScan, a real-time analysis pipeline employing hierarchical basecalling and OTU-level consensus generation to achieve high-accuracy taxonomic assignments during sequencing. Using a single set of universal primers, we integrate metabarcoding and barcoding into a cohesive protocol, utilizing universal markers for both animals and plants (cytochrome oxidase 1 region, COI, and Internal Transcribed Spacer 2, ITS2). This comprehensive approach can detect and identify a broad spectrum of species, from individual organisms to entire communities in a single workflow.

papers.title: Natural isolates of Sinorhizobium meliloti with dry, as opposed to mucoid, colony morphologies have higher soil fitness, slightly lower host fitness, and reduced nitrogen fixation
papers.abstract: Sinorhizobium meliloti is a nitrogen-fixing soil bacterium that forms a facultative mutualism with its host alfalfa. S. meliloti strains exhibit diverse colony morphologies on solid culture media that span a continuum from dry to mucoid. Studies on how this trait affects symbiosis rely on mutations in exopolysaccharide II production genes; however, whether natural variation in morphology confers a selective advantage on rhizobia in their natural habitats remains unknown. Here, we used 90 mucoid and 27 dry natural isolates to test whether colony morphology is associated with rhizobial fitness in the soil and in the host, or with the nitrogen-fixation benefits they provide to the plant. Colony morphologies were widely distributed across a phylogenetic tree, suggesting that morphological shifts occurred repeatedly and no single genetic variant was strongly associated with this trait. We inoculated soil mesocosms and plants with a mixture of dry and mucoid bacteria. We observed that dry rhizobia have higher fitness, particularly at 22{degrees}C and 32{degrees}C, but not under cold or drought conditions, independent of the initial rhizobial load. Conversely, mucoid bacteria have a modestly higher relative fitness in host nodules, and single inoculations showed that they tend to confer greater benefits to all three alfalfa varieties. Over time, we also observed rare, repeated conversion from mucoid to dry morphologies in soil and host plants. Taken together, our study reveals that morphological variation within a species in a single agricultural field is important for bacterial fitness in the soil and can have cascading effects on the rhizobia's plant benefits.

papers.title: Active late Holocene accretion of mesophotic coral-rubble fields in the northern Red Sea
papers.abstract: Mesophotic coral ecosystems are commonly interpreted as thin biological veneers over relict shallow-water reef structures, but their capacity to generate late Holocene carbonate deposits remains poorly quantified. Here we combine diver excavations, rubble-bed thickness surveys, radiocarbon age-depth modelling, sediment grain-size analyses, coral-rubble assemblages, trace-element geochemistry, and modern Alveopora allingi growth measurements from two 40-65 m deep coral-rubble fields in the northern Gulf of Eilat/Aqaba, Red Sea. Rubble deposits are at least 1.0-1.5 m thick and accumulated at mean rates of 2.21 {+/-} 0.52 mm yr-1 at the Dekel site and 1.33 {+/-} 0.13 mm yr-1 at the IUI site, implying persistent carbonate accumulation over centuries to >1 kyr. Age-depth models indicate quasi-continuous deposition despite pronounced faunal changes, including a shift from A. allingi-dominated rubble to upper layers enriched in Euphyllia paradivisa at Dekel. The dominant modern rubble-forming coral, A. allingi, extends at 3.04 {+/-} 0.87 mm yr-1 and has skeletal density of 1.17 {+/-} 0.27 g cm-3. First-order cover-based accretion estimates at present coral cover fall well below the radiocarbon-derived rates, indicating that long-term mesophotic rubble accumulation integrates historical cover, secondary calcification and sediment retention rather than present live coral cover alone. These data demonstrate that mesophotic rubble fields can act as active carbonate factories and palaeoecological archives, challenging the assumption that modern mesophotic habitats are geomorphologically passive.

papers.title: Assessment of trace metals and arsenic contamination in water and sediments in a former mining area of the river basin after an ecological disaster, Slana River, Slovakia
papers.abstract: This study assesses the spatial dynamics of heavy metals and associated trace elements in the water and sediment of the Slana River approximately one and half year after an environmental accident and river contamination caused by mining effluent. Using PCA and standardized environmental indices (CF, PLI), we modelled the distribution of contaminants across the macro-gradient of the river and within the micro-gradient surrounding the source of pollution. We found that although the situation in the water column has improved and stabilized, the sediment remains the primary reservoir of trace elements, including toxic arsenic, with the highest concentrations recorded near the source and in its immediate vicinity. Although the concentration of primary mining indicators decreases relatively rapidly along the stream, this is systematically offset by the accumulation of other elements, including sulphur and aluminium. As a result of these geochemical processes, the total pollution load index (PLI) remains statistically unchanged along the entire stream, but indicates a chronic, spatially uniform (PLI = 1.06-1.16) toxicological burden on the ecosystem.

papers.title: Conservation value of secondary and plantation forests for fruit-feeding butterflies in northern Vietnam
papers.abstract: 1. Assessing the conservation value of secondary forests and reforestation is important for conservation planning. Butterflies are widely used as indicators, and fruit-feeding butterflies are often used in biodiversity assessments in tropical landscapes. 2. We examined fruit-feeding butterfly diversity, abundance, and community composition across a primary forest, a secondary forest, and a plantation forest in northern Vietnam. We sampled butterflies nearly monthly during one year using baited traps. 3. Primary and secondary forest supported higher species richness than plantation forest. Moreover, while secondary forest had mainly a subset of species found in primary forest, the plantation forest had a distinct butterfly fauna. 4. Butterfly abundance and community composition varied across months, without showing a clear seasonal pattern. 5. Our results suggest that secondary and plantation forests do not fully replace primary forests, but they contribute meaningfully to butterfly conservation in human-modified tropical landscapes.

papers.title: Soil invertebrate biomass estimation from image-derived body area and contour length
papers.abstract: 1. Soil invertebrate biomass is closely linked to ecosystem processes, yet its routine quantification remains constrained by the effort required to weigh large numbers of small individuals. Length-mass relationships provide an indirect alternative, but body length can be difficult to standardise and extract automatically from images of curved, coiled or contracted organisms. Projected body area may provide a more tractable image-derived predictor, but its performance across diverse soil-faunal taxa and at the community scale remains insufficiently evaluated. 2. Here, we developed a framework using projected body area and contour length to estimate fresh and dry mass from measurements of 1,792 soil invertebrates representing 15 higher-level taxa. We fitted taxon-specific models for six well-represented groups and general models across taxa, and evaluated predictive performance using leave-one-out cross-validation. We then assessed cross-dataset transferability by comparing our data with those of Lemoine et al. (2026) and pooled the two datasets to derive combined models. Finally, we tested whether individual predictions could be scaled to independently measured community biomass. 3. Taxon-specific models generally reduced prediction error relative to general models, with mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) values of 6.9-37.3% for fresh mass and 7.6-30.2% for dry mass. General models retained MAPEs of 27.2% and 22.4%, respectively. Comparisons of our dataset with that of Lemoine et al. (2026) showed no detectable differences in six of eight taxon-by-mass slopes. Although intercepts frequently differed, no overall dataset effect was detected after accounting for taxa. Pooling both datasets broadened model development, while taxon-specific models generally retained lower error than the combined general model. Finally, community-level predictions tracked measured biomass across all model sets (R2 = 0.87-0.99), but absolute error varied among models and faunal groups (MAPE = 9.6-52.5%). 4. Body area and contour length extracted from images therefore provide a practical basis for scaling soil invertebrate biomass estimation from individuals to communities. Integration with automated imaging and segmentation tools such as flatbug, BIODISCOVER and CollembolAI could extend soil invertebrate monitoring at larger scales beyond abundance and taxonomic composition to biomass, while providing scalable inputs for analyses of food webs and general ecosystem ecology.
